analysis.headline: The 3-year fps delay (EIS 2041 to 2044) makes COMAC only slightly more likely to become a material third player outside China. My estimate for at least 100 C919-class exports a year by 2045 rises from about 7% to about 9% (+2 pp). If the definition's "funded programme by 2035" prong is read as an export-oriented new single-aisle, the odds go from about 17% to about 23% (+6 pp). Read literally, that prong is already met by the C919 (launched 2008, 158-192 seats), so the definition cannot tell the two worlds apart. These are judgements. The binding constraints are not the size of the board's vacuum. They are COMAC's ramp (15 deliveries in 2025, 3 in Q1 2026, none in September 2026), US-controlled parts (LEAP-1C licences suspended in 2025; COMAC parts licences capped from October 2026) and EASA validation (no earlier than 2028-31). The much likelier effect is COMAC taking over Boeing's China share: I estimate about 45% rising to about 52% that COMAC supplies at least 40% of China's single-aisle deliveries by 2045. That does not count as a third player, but on the board it is the bigger threat. Removing just 6.2% of the 2,000/yr market from Boeing and Airbus erases the snapshot's +1.06 fps case at 2041.

The programme was launched in 2008, got its CAAC type certificate on 29 Sep 2022, made its first delivery on 9 Dec 2022 and entered service on 28 May 2023. capability_facts.fact: Boeing's 2045 NB share is 33% with fps in 2041, 22% with fps in 2044 and 20% under Do Nothing. Airbus overflow above its capacity in 2045: at 1,200/yr it is 140 (fps 2041), 360 (fps 2044) and 400 (Do Nothing); at 900/yr it is 440, 660 and 700. PV-2026 of 1 pp of global NB share over 2041-2056 at board prices, margins and WACCs: Airbus NGSA $0.87B, Boeing fps $0.53B, A320neo $0.41B, Boeing 737 $0.14B.
Calhoun: "even in an optimistic case, maybe in 2050, they get to be a 10% player". He also said the duopoly would last "for quite some time" before China is "accepted in the world".

entry_paths.path: Independent: an EASA-validated C919 (LEAP-1C) exported at scale to mainstream airlines and lessors, partly financed by Chinese lessors and policy banks. This is the main route to the definition's export prong.
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Board fact: Boeing's 2045 share is 33% with fps in 2041 and 22% with fps in 2044. Airbus overflow above 1,200/yr in 2045 is 140 vs 360, so the delay adds 176 aircraft a year outside China. Judgement: the C919 is a LEAP-generation aircraft, on a par with the 737 MAX and a generation behind NGSA and fps. With no new Boeing aircraft until 2044, or ever (fps drops out of every equilibrium from 2043), the C919's only same-generation rival is a 737 with no successor, and airlines facing an Airbus near-monopoly want a second source. I put the probability of at least 100 exports a year, given capacity, supply and certification, at 0.40 in the 2041 world and 0.52 in the 2044 world. Not higher, because China's own airlines will also want more C919s once Boeing weakens, which competes with exports for COMAC's output.
binding_constraints: Production: COMAC needs about 250-300/yr by 2045 (its domestic share plus 100 exports) against 15 in 2025 and near zero since spring 2026. I put this at 0.37 / 0.39.
US-controlled parts and engines: LEAP-1C licences were suspended May-July 2025 and COMAC parts licences have been capped since October 2026. I put no multi-year cap on the ramp at 0.65 / 0.63.
EASA validation by about 2038: EASA's own window is 2028-31, and lessors' residual values depend on it. 0.72 / 0.74.
Product support, MRO network and residual-value acceptance outside China, where COMAC has no record for the C919.

entry_paths.path: Independent: export to politically aligned or CAAC-accepting markets without EASA validation (the C909 pattern: Laos, Cambodia, Brunei, Indonesia), with a CJ-1000A version for sanctioned markets
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Judgement: these markets are small and mostly served by lessors that need EASA or FAA paper. The C909's total foreign fleet is single digits after 10 years (5 TransNusa, 2 Lao, 20 Air Cambodia on order). A weaker Boeing adds a little political room, since fewer Boeing-for-trade deals compete in these markets. Reaching 100/yr without EASA stays a long shot in both worlds.
binding_constraints: Market size: aligned or CAAC-accepting carriers take far fewer than 100 single-aisles a year from any one supplier.
The CJ-1000A is not in mass production until about 2030 (OAG) and has no foreign certification.
Lessor financing and remarketing need EASA or FAA validation.

entry_paths.path: Independent: funded launch by 2035 of a new export-oriented 150-210-seat single-aisle (a C919 successor or major derivative with a Western certification basis). This is the definition's second prong under my substantive reading.
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Judgement: the launch window closes in 2035. A Boeing new aircraft for 2041 would be launched around 2033-34; one for 2044 around 2036-37 or never. So in the 2041 world COMAC decides after Boeing has committed and faces two new-generation incumbents. In the 2044 world it decides while Boeing has nothing new, which makes a next-generation 'second source to NGSA' more attractive to Beijing. Limits: COMAC is also funding the C919 ramp and the C929 (CAAC type certificate goal 2032, service by 2035), and an export-grade next-generation engine is unlikely to be licensed from the West.
binding_constraints: Engineering bandwidth shared with the C919 ramp and C929 development
A next-generation engine: the CJ-1000A is LEAP-generation, and the US is unlikely to license newer engine technology
Political willingness to commit state funds before the C919 has proved itself abroad

entry_paths.path: COMAC takes over Boeing's China share (domestic only), defined as at least 40% of China's single-aisle deliveries by 2045 (about 160/yr). This is part (a) and does NOT meet the definition.
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Facts: China is about 20% of single-aisle demand. China's Boeing orders are visibly a trade-deal currency: 200 aircraft confirmed after the May 2026 summit, up to 750 cited, with spare parts used as US leverage in October 2026. Judgement: with Boeing at 20-22% globally and no new aircraft, the commercial case for 737s in China weakens. Beijing keeps buying politically negotiated Boeing tranches but steers organic growth to COMAC and to Airbus Tianjin, whose second line delivered first on 16 Sep 2026. This happens largely regardless of fps timing. It mainly gives COMAC scale, which feeds the export paths.
binding_constraints: The same production and US-parts constraints as the export paths, with a lower bar
Chinese airlines' 2025-26 experience of C919 delays (they expected 33 in 2026)
US-China trade deals that tie Boeing purchases to tariff and export-control relief

entry_paths.path: Partnership routes that create no third player: Boeing + Embraer (the board's fps via Embraer Joint Venture) or any Boeing-COMAC cooperation
entry_paths.p_fps_2041: <1% for a Boeing-COMAC Joint Venture; the Embraer Joint Venture is dominated on the board
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Board fact: fps via Embraer ($100B) minus Do Nothing is -17.05 at 2041 and -15.95 at 2044, never chosen, with break-even capex of $52.9B. Even if chosen, it is Boeing's product and adds no third player. Judgement: a Boeing-COMAC Joint Venture is politically ruled out (COMAC has been on a DoD Chinese-military-company list since Jan 2021, plus US export controls), and Boeing executives have long warned against trading IP for access (BX-0678).
binding_constraints: US export controls and national-security politics
The board's Joint Venture economics (via Embraer capex $100B vs break-even $52.9B)

overall.definition: Third player = a company other than Boeing or Airbus (here COMAC) that, by 2045, delivers at least 100 single-aisles of 150-210 seats a year (5% of the board's 2,000/yr) to customers outside mainland China (Hong Kong and Macau count as home), OR has committed funding by 2035 to such a programme. Read literally, the second prong is already met by the C919 (launched 2008, 158-192 seats), which gives about 100% in both worlds and a zero delay effect; that reading cannot discriminate. I therefore score the second prong as a funded, export-oriented NEW or substantially re-engineered single-aisle launched by 2035. Core metric (export prong only): about 7% (2041) vs about 9% (2044). Lenient reading (at least 100/yr in total with some exports): judgement about 45% vs about 48%.
overall.p_fps_2044: ~23% (judgemental range 13-35%). Export prong alone ~9% (4-18%). Delay effect +6 pp (range +2 to +10); export prong alone +2.3 pp (range +1 to +5).
overall.method: (1) Opportunity, from the board's own share rule (my solve, scratchpad/wf/comac/board_comac.json). Airbus overflow above 1,200/yr in 2045 is 140 (fps 2041) vs 360 (fps 2044); the delay adds 220/yr in 2045 (176 outside China) and 2,000 aircraft over 2041-2050. On board conventions an entrant's NPV moves from -2.78 to -0.51. Where I disagree (judgement): (a) the overflow is not COMAC's to take. The board lets Boeing deliver only 20-22% (400-440/yr), yet Boeing built 447 737s in 2025, so the 737 absorbs most overflow, with Airbus capacity growth and life extensions taking the rest. I treat about a quarter to a third of the ex-China overflow as contestable by a validated C919. (b) About 20% of the board's market is China, which COMAC fills first. (c) The NPV gate does not bind COMAC: its development cost is sunk and it is state-funded (44bn yuan in Nov 2025). Its binding constraints are production, parts politics, certification and acceptance. (d) 2,000/yr is above the 2026-2045 average in Boeing's and Airbus's forecasts (about 1,680-1,710/yr), though plausible for the 2040s. (2) Export-prong chain, as triangular (low, mode, high) for 2041 / 2044. L1 production of about 250-300/yr by 2045: 0.22, 0.37, 0.52 / 0.24, 0.39, 0.54. L2 Western parts and engine supply not capped for years, or domestic substitutes ready: 0.45, 0.65, 0.80 / 0.43, 0.63, 0.78 (a weaker Boeing makes Washington more protective). L3 EASA validation and market access by about 2038: 0.55, 0.72, 0.85 / 0.57, 0.74, 0.86. L4 commercial pull plus allocating at least 100/yr to exports: 0.25, 0.40, 0.55 / 0.35, 0.52, 0.68. The product of the modes is 0.069 / 0.095. (3) Second prong (substantive): 0.05, 0.12, 0.22 / 0.08, 0.17, 0.28. Union = P1 + P2 - P(P2|P1) x P1, with P(P2|P1) 0.30, 0.45, 0.60. (4) Monte Carlo with 200k draws and the same random numbers in both worlds (scratchpad/wf/comac/chain_mc.py, chain_mc.json). Means and p10-p90: export prong 6.6% (4.5-9.0) vs 8.9% (6.2-12.0); union 16.6% (11.9-21.7) vs 22.6% (16.9-28.4); delay effect +2.3 pp (export prong) and +5.9 pp (union). A correlated version with link correlation 0.6 widens the export prong to 3.5-11.2% vs 4.9-14.7% (chain_mc_corr.json). The ranges quoted above are widened further for model uncertainty. Every link value is judgement anchored on the facts listed; nothing here is a board output.

leading_indicators: C919 deliveries: 2026 against COMAC's plan of about 28 and IBA's 25 (only 3 by Q1, none in Sep 2026). Raise the odds if deliveries exceed 60 in 2028 and 100 in 2030 (IBA has 59 and 93); cut them if 2027-28 stays under 40.
EASA validation: completion inside EASA's 2028-31 window, then any FAA validation activity. No EASA validation by 2032 roughly halves the export prong.

US export licensing: whether the October 2026 cap on COMAC parts licences becomes a formal rule (landing gear and similar), and how the US-China tariff truce due in November 2026 ends. A renewed LEAP-1C suspension like May-July 2025 would be a strong negative.
CJ-1000A: its CAAC type certificate (OAG expects 2027-28), the first C919 delivered with it, and whether export C919s stay on LEAP-1C. That decides CFM's share of COMAC's growth.

First firm C919 orders from non-Chinese airlines beyond GallopAir's 2023 letter of intent, especially Southeast Asian low-cost carriers, Middle East or African carriers, or Chinese lessors (BOC Aviation, CDB Aviation, ICBC Leasing) placing C919s with foreign operators.
Boeing's fps launch decision: a launch around 2033-34 for 2041 versus silence. Also Boeing's 737 rate (447 delivered in 2025) as the overflow absorber the board ignores.
Airbus capacity: A320-family rate beyond 75/month and the backlog length in years, which together size the real overflow.

China's procurement split: whether the Boeing 200 (up to 750) tranches firm up, the C919 share of Chinese single-aisle deliveries, and further CAAC actions on Airbus approvals tied to C919 certification.

Further state capital for COMAC (after 44bn yuan in Nov 2025), new C919 assembly capacity (plan 150/yr by 2028), and any announcement of a next-generation single-aisle programme or a C919 stretch or re-wing.
analysis.impact_on_game: 1) Part (a), COMAC taking China, is the bigger lever on the board, and it is largely independent of the delay. Board solve (scratchpad/wf/comac/board_comac.json): I shrank the 2,000/yr market seen by Boeing and Airbus by x and re-solved with overlap strain. In the modal context (Airbus NGSA + Re-engine A350, Boeing Do Nothing 787), fps 10-yr minus Do Nothing at 2041 goes +1.06 (x=0), +0.21 (5%), +0.01 (6.2%, break-even), -0.64 (10%), -1.50 (15%), -2.35 (20%), about -0.17 per point. Against Airbus Delay Tactics it is already -0.24 at x=0 and -1.82 at 10%. Equilibria at 2041: 0 pure / 17 near-Nash at x=0. At 5%: 1 pure + 10 near, fps 10-yr in 6. At 10%: 2 pure + 3 near, fps in 1. At 15% or more, fps is in none. At 2044 fps is already out of every equilibrium; fps minus Do Nothing goes -2.53, -2.99 (5%), -3.46 (10%), -4.39 (20%). China is about 20% of single-aisle demand, so COMAC winning 30-50% of China (x of about 6-10%) is enough on its own to turn the snapshot's fps case negative. This takes the duopoly's market proportionally, which is a simplification. A C919 is a 737-generation rival, so in reality it erodes the Do Nothing 737 more than fps, which would partly offset this; the 737 is worth only $0.14B per point of share vs $0.53B for fps. 2) Airbus: its payoff vs Boeing Do Nothing falls from +50.12 to +43.96 at x=10% and +37.80 at 20%. The board charges Airbus about $0.87B per point of NGSA share, but if Airbus is capacity-bound (about 900/yr per its FY2025 report vs the board's 1,600/yr), COMAC exports mostly fill overflow Airbus could not build, so the real cost is smaller. Judgement: in the delay world Europe has less reason to slow-walk C919 validation, and China already pressures Airbus approvals to that end. 3) Procurement politics (judgement): a weaker Boeing (20-22% from 2043) turns Boeing orders in China into pure trade-deal currency (200 confirmed, up to 750 cited, spare parts used as US leverage in October 2026). Organic Chinese growth then goes to COMAC and Airbus Tianjin. That raises COMAC's domestic scale, a modest plus for exports, but also absorbs C919 output that could have been exported. It also raises the US incentive to choke COMAC's US content to protect Boeing, as the October 2026 parts caps show. Net: export odds are only slightly higher. 4) CFM (facts: LEAP-1C sole source on the C919; CFM on both NGSA and fps; engine board unchanged by the delay because engine NB EIS = min(fps, NGSA) = 2037; war-game CFM +18.99 delayed vs +18.75 on time). Judgement: CFM gains from COMAC as an exporter, because export C919s will carry LEAP-1C and every overflow aircraft filled by a C919 is 2 CFM engines rather than an old aircraft kept flying. It is neutral against a 737 sale (LEAP-1B is also 100% CFM). It loses from COMAC as a domestic substitute once the CJ-1000A arrives (about 2030): each Chinese 737 (100% CFM) or neo replaced by a CJ-1000A C919 is lost. The delay shifts about 11 points of 2045 share away from Boeing; if China's roughly 20% of that (about 44 aircraft a year) goes to CJ-1000A C919s, CFM loses about 88 engines a year, roughly 2% of NB engines. CFM is also the US's chosen chokepoint (licences suspended in 2025, allocation squeezed in 2026), so its COMAC revenue is hostage to policy. Net: slightly negative for CFM after about 2035 in the delay world, unless COMAC exports at scale on LEAP-1C. The board cannot value any of this because it has no COMAC. 5) Modelling fix suggested: add an Airbus capacity cap and a non-strategic COMAC fringe share (China share s_CN(t) plus a slice of ex-China overflow), and let the 737 absorb overflow. Without this, the board overstates both the vacuum and Airbus's capturable gain.

check.overall:
The analysis mostly holds up but needs material corrections. Facts first. I re-ran every board number (wf/adv_comac/rerun.py gives output byte-identical to wf/comac/board_comac.json; eqcheck.py reproduces the equilibrium counts). The vacuum.json entrant NPVs, the PV per point of share, the snapshot inputs and every repo evidence citation (CX-0168/1098/1197, BX-0380/0280/0022/0062/0657/0678, B-1302, P-1287, AX-0024, A-0865) are accurate. Most web facts are confirmed with dated sources: the LEAP-1C suspension May-July 2025, the 1 Oct 2026 Reuters story on capped COMAC parts licences and the possible landing-gear rule, the 200-aircraft Boeing commitment, the CAAC holding about 20 Airbus approvals, the Tianjin second-line delivery on 16 Sep 2026, Boeing's 447 737s in 2025, the CMO/GMF figures with China at about 20%, EASA's 3-6 years, the C929 dates, and the Ulaanbaatar route.

Factual errors to fix:
- The Air Cambodia order is 20 C909s, not 10+10, and TransNusa operates 3 C909s, not 5.
- 2024 C919 deliveries were 10-13 depending on source.
- COMAC was not continuously on a DoD list from Jan 2021; it was delisted and then re-listed in Jan 2025.
- The analysis quotes two different IBA 2026 forecasts (25 and 28).
- 'None in September 2026', which is in the headline, could not be verified.

Framing and judgement problems:
1. The vacuum comparison uses fps launched in 2044, although the analyst's own equilibrium logic says Boeing does Do Nothing. This understates the delay effect: +260/yr (not +220) and +2,560 cumulative (not +2,000).
2. 'x = 6-10% turns fps negative' is wrong at the low end, where 6% is break-even.
3. There are internal inconsistencies. Path 2 is carved out of a chain whose L3 requires EASA. Path 4 is called 'largely regardless of fps timing' but moves +7 pp. The CFM loss assumes 100% CFM content.
4. The chain's conditioning is unstated. If L1 is unconditional on parts, the export prong is about 11% → 15%, not 7% → 9%.
5. Most of the +6 pp union effect comes from the least-evidenced judgement (prong 2).

Missed evidence:
- Our own war game puts Boeing at 32% in 2045 in the delay case, not 20-22%, so the vacuum is smaller.
- AirAsia's confirmed C919 talks and Malaysia Airlines' evaluation.
- The July 2026 report that EASA flight tests are wrapping up with no major hardware risks.
- The fragility of the Boeing 200 deal.

Judgement on the conclusions: the qualitative conclusions survive.
